state.legal_review_memo:
PRIVILEGED - LEGAL REVIEW MEMO
To: Procurement (IT Services category)
From: Commercial Legal (A. Mensah)
Re: Kitefin Logistics Software - Master Services Agreement, vendor redlines of 16 Sep

1. Summary
Kitefin returned our MSA template with seven redlines. Two are acceptable, four need to go back to the vendor, and one needs escalation to the Legal Director before we can respond. Nothing in the redlines touches the data processing agreement, which Kitefin accepted in full.

2. Clause-by-clause
2.1 Limitation of liability (cl. 12.1). Our template caps each party's liability at the fees paid in the prior 12 months. Kitefin proposes 6 months. The playbook fallback allows nothing below 12 months for systems that run operational processes, and this platform will run warehouse dispatch. Push back.
2.2 IP indemnity (cl. 13). Kitefin accepted our standard wording. No action.
2.3 Renewal (cl. 15.2). Our template renews for 12-month terms. Kitefin proposes 24-month renewal terms. The playbook fallback allows only 12-month renewal terms. Push back.
2.4 Payment terms (cl. 8.3). Our template is net 45. Kitefin proposes net 30. The playbook allows net 30 for suppliers that qualify as SMEs under our supplier definition. Kitefin's account director confirmed by email that Kitefin qualifies as an SME; we have not seen accounts. Accept, on that basis.
2.5 Audit rights (cl. 17). Our template allows audits on reasonable notice. The playbook fallback allows limiting audits to once per year, provided an additional audit is always permitted after a security incident. Kitefin's version limits audits to once per year and deletes the post-incident audit. Push back and reinstate the incident audit.
2.6 Governing law (cl. 24). Kitefin proposes its home jurisdiction. The playbook requires our governing law unless the Legal Director approves otherwise; I do not recommend asking for that here. Push back.
2.7 Termination for convenience (cl. 16.3). Kitefin deleted our right to terminate for convenience entirely. There is no playbook fallback for this clause; removal is outside my authority to accept. Escalate to the Legal Director before any response goes to Kitefin.

3. Recommendation
Accept 2.2 and 2.4. Send 2.1, 2.3, 2.5 and 2.6 back with our fallback positions. Hold the response until the Legal Director has considered 2.7. Please do not share this memo with the vendor.

A. Mensah, Senior Commercial Counsel

state: P-card review note - card ending 4471 (holder: D. Mercer, Facilities). Two transactions at Harlow Hardware Supplies on the same afternoon, 14:02 and 14:09, both described as 'site safety barriers', and each just under the single-transaction limit according to the card platform's flag. Cardholder explanation: 'The shop's card machine declined the full amount, so the cashier split it into two.' No receipt or merchant statement confirming a declined attempt was provided. The barriers were needed to cordon off an unplanned chemical spill in the loading bay; the Facilities manager confirms the spill happened that afternoon. Policy PC-4 prohibits splitting a purchase to stay under the single-transaction limit. Policy PC-7 allows emergency purchases above the limit on a single transaction, with retrospective manager approval within 2 working days. No PC-7 approval was sought.

split_pattern.instructions: Does the note describe a pattern consistent with a split purchase?

explanation_documented.instructions: Is the cardholder's explanation supported by documentation mentioned in the note?

likely_cause.instructions: What best explains the two transactions on the information in the note?

criteria.emergency_without_using_pc7: A genuine emergency handled without the PC-7 route

pc7_available.instructions: Would PC-7 have offered a compliant way to make this purchase?

severity.instructions: How serious is this P-card finding?

criteria.definition: Nothing wrong
A lapse with a genuine business need
A probable policy breach needing a formal warning
Suspected misuse or fraud

split_pattern.note: Same merchant, same item, seven minutes apart, each just under the limit is the classic split pattern, whatever the cause.

explanation_documented.note: 'No receipt or merchant statement confirming a declined attempt was provided.'

likely_cause.note: The spill is confirmed, which makes an emergency handled clumsily most plausible. The merchant story is unverified and deliberate evasion isn't excluded, so the undeterminable reading is close behind.

pc7_available.note: A confirmed unplanned spill looks like the emergency PC-7 covers, so a single over-limit transaction with retrospective approval was available. Whether barrier purchases count as an emergency is a judgement some would not make.

severity.note: A genuine emergency need supports a procedural lapse, but the split pattern plus an undocumented excuse pushes some reviewers to a probable breach.

state.supplier_questionnaire:
Responsible Sourcing Questionnaire - Tamsin Textiles Ltd (apparel supplier, tier 1)

Q1. Do you publish a modern slavery or forced labour statement?
A1. Yes, published annually on our website and signed by our managing director.

Q2. How do you audit your own factories?
A2. Our two garment factories are audited annually by an accredited third-party social compliance auditor. The latest audits found minor findings on fire exit signage, since closed.

Q3. How do you assess your own suppliers (tier 2, e.g. fabric mills and dye houses)?
A3. Tier 2 suppliers complete our self-assessment questionnaire every two years. We do not currently audit tier 2 sites.

Q4. Do workers pay any fees to obtain employment?
A4. We do not charge workers recruitment fees. Some of the labour agents we use for seasonal staff charge workers a registration fee; we are phasing these agents out over the next two seasons.

Q5. Do you hold workers' identity documents?
A5. No. Workers keep their own documents; lockers are provided.

Q6. What are your working-hours practices?
A6. Overtime is voluntary and capped in line with local law. During peak season some lines exceed the legal cap with the written consent of workers, and all overtime is paid at premium rates.

Q7. Do you have a grievance mechanism?
A7. Yes, an anonymous hotline in the three main languages spoken by our workers, run by an external provider.

Q8. Have you had to remediate any forced labour or child labour cases?
A8. No remediation has been required to date.

Q9. Do you subcontract production?
A9. Only embroidery, to two approved subcontractors listed in our supplier register.

Q10. How are wages paid?
A10. Monthly, by bank transfer, with itemised payslips. Seasonal staff recruited through agents are paid by the agent, who deducts accommodation where workers use agent-provided housing.

Q11. Do you provide worker accommodation?
A11. We do not operate dormitories. Some agent-recruited seasonal staff live in housing arranged by the agents; we have not inspected it.

Q12. Are your audit reports available to customers?
A12. Summary reports are available on request under NDA.

Q13. Do you audit or monitor your labour agents?
A13. Agents sign our code of conduct when appointed. We have not audited them; we rely on worker feedback through the hotline, which has received no complaints about agents this year.

Q14. Any other information?
A14. We are working towards an industry sustainability certification next year.

ENHANCED DUE DILIGENCE REPORT - Coastline Port Services SARL
Prepared for: Group Procurement, Port Logistics category
Purpose: proposed three-year contract for stevedoring and customs brokerage at the Port of Selmar (Republic of Veltria).

1. Corporate profile. Coastline Port Services SARL is a privately held company incorporated in Veltria in 2012, with around 180 employees. Registered shareholders: Yusuf Karan (70%) and Coastline Holdings Ltd (30%), a holding company in the Kingdom of Morland whose sole shareholder is also Yusuf Karan. Directors: Yusuf Karan (managing director) and Leyla Karan.

2. Politically exposed persons. Leyla Karan, a director, is the spouse of Emre Karan, the current Deputy Minister of Transport of Veltria, whose ministry oversees port concessions and licenses customs brokers. Leyla Karan has held her directorship since 2015, before her husband's appointment in 2023. No other PEP connections were identified.

3. Sanctions. Company, shareholders and directors were screened against the synthetic consolidated lists used by the Group; no matches.

4. Adverse media. No adverse media on the company or its directors was found in English, French or local-language sources covering the last ten years. One 2021 trade press article praised the company's safety record.

5. Contract context. The contract would require the vendor to obtain port access permits and customs brokerage licences from authorities under the Ministry of Transport. The Group would be the largest customer of the vendor.

6. Financial overview. Filed accounts for the last three years show steady revenue growth and modest profits. The auditor's opinions were unqualified. The company has no outstanding tax disputes on the public record.

7. References. Two current customers (a regional shipping line and a fruit importer) described the company as reliable and well connected at the port. One said the company 'always gets permits through quickly', which the analyst notes could reflect efficiency or influence and should be explored in interviews.

8. Analyst assessment. The PEP connection is significant given the ministry's direct role in licensing the services being purchased. There is no indication of wrongdoing. Recommended mitigations: anti-bribery contractual clauses with audit rights, a certification that no payments are made to public officials, and annual refresh of this report. Senior management approval is required under the Group's third-party policy for any vendor with a PEP connection in a role relevant to the contract.

9. Next steps. Interviews with the managing director and Leyla Karan are proposed before contract award, covering how permits are obtained, any contact with the Ministry, and whether Leyla Karan would step back from government-facing work during the contract.

state.panel_minutes:
MINUTES - Tender Panel, RFP-2026-048 Facilities Management (Northern sites)
Present: H. Okoye (Chair, Procurement), R. Singh (Facilities), M. Duarte (Finance), P. Kowalczyk (Health & Safety), L. Brennan (Estates)

1. Declarations of interest. None declared at the start of the meeting. The Chair reminded members that interests arising during the meeting must be declared immediately.

2. Technical scores. The panel reviewed the moderated technical scores. Brightstone FM ranked first on technical quality, Harwell Services second and Ostara Facilities third. P. Kowalczyk noted that Ostara's safety method statements were the weakest of the three and would need significant work before mobilisation. L. Brennan commented that Harwell's estates maintenance approach was 'the most practical of the three' and argued for raising its moderated score on question 4; the panel agreed a one-point increase. R. Singh noted that Brightstone's staffing model was the most resilient, with named relief staff at every site.

3. Commercial scores. M. Duarte presented the commercial evaluation. Ostara was the lowest price, Harwell second and Brightstone the most expensive. Combined weighted scores placed Harwell first overall, Brightstone a close second and Ostara third. M. Duarte observed that the margin between the top two was narrow enough that small scoring changes could reverse it.

4. Declaration during the meeting. During the discussion of Harwell's mobilisation plan, L. Brennan declared that her former line manager is now Harwell's regional director and that they remain in regular contact socially. The Chair asked L. Brennan to leave the meeting for the remainder of the Harwell discussion and the recommendation vote. L. Brennan left the meeting.

5. Recommendation. The remaining members voted on the recommendation. H. Okoye, M. Duarte and P. Kowalczyk supported an award to Harwell Services. R. Singh preferred Brightstone FM, citing its stronger technical score and his concern about Harwell's staffing levels at the two largest sites, and asked for his dissent to be minuted. The Chair confirmed the panel remained quorate after L. Brennan's departure.

6. Actions. Procurement to update the conflicts register with L. Brennan's declaration; Procurement to prepare the award recommendation report for the Category Board; R. Singh's concerns about staffing to be raised with Harwell at clarification.

7. Any other business. None.

Minutes approved by: H. Okoye (Chair)

state.software_policy: SW-P1 Any SaaS that will store personal data requires a security and privacy review before use, regardless of cost. SW-P2 Tools with click-through terms still need Legal review of those terms. SW-P3 Special-category personal data (including health information) also requires a data protection impact assessment. SW-P4 Purchases with no cost do not need a PO but must be registered in the software inventory.

po_needed.instructions: Does `software_policy` require a PO for this tool?

review_needed.instructions: Does `software_policy` require a security and privacy review before use?

special_category.instructions: Could the data described in `request` include special-category data under SW-P3?

steps_required.instructions: Which set of steps does `software_policy` require before the tool is used?

requester_understanding.instructions: How accurate is the requester's understanding of what's needed?

criteria.definition: Fully accurate
Mostly accurate, minor omission
Right about the PO but unaware of the reviews
Wrong on every point

po_needed.note: SW-P4: no-cost purchases need no PO.

review_needed.note: Names and emails are personal data, so SW-P1 applies regardless of cost.

special_category.note: Dietary and accessibility needs can reveal health information (allergies, disabilities), which SW-P3 names. Some dietary preferences are not health data.

steps_required.note: Inventory (P4), terms review (P2) and security/privacy review (P1) all apply, plus a DPIA (P3) if accessibility or health needs count as special-category, which most would say they do.

requester_understanding.note: The requester is right that no PO is needed but unaware of the reviews.

offboarding_checklist: OFF-V1 All vendor user accounts and VPN/SSO access disabled
OFF-V2 Company data returned in an agreed format
OFF-V3 Certificate of data deletion signed by the vendor
OFF-V5 Final invoice reconciled and no open POs
